    27	## Requests and limits
    28	
    29	If the node where a Pod is running has enough of a resource available, it's possible (and
    30	allowed) for a container to use more resource than its `request` for that resource specifies.
    31	
    32	For example, if you set a `memory` request of 256 MiB for a container, and that container is in
    33	a Pod scheduled to a Node with 8GiB of memory and no other Pods, then the container can try to use
    34	more RAM.
    35	
    36	Limits are a different story. Both `cpu` and `memory` limits are applied by the kubelet (and
    37	{{< glossary_tooltip text="container runtime" term_id="container-runtime" >}}),
    38	and are ultimately enforced by the kernel. On Linux nodes, the Linux kernel
    39	enforces limits with
    40	{{< glossary_tooltip text="cgroups" term_id="cgroup" >}}.
    41	The behavior of `cpu` and `memory` limit enforcement is slightly different.
    42	
    43	`cpu` limits are enforced by CPU throttling. When a container approaches
    44	its `cpu` limit, the kernel will restrict access to the CPU corresponding to the
    45	container's limit. Thus, a `cpu` limit is a hard limit the kernel enforces.
    46	Containers may not use more CPU than is specified in their `cpu` limit.
    47	
    48	`memory` limits are enforced by the kernel with out of memory (OOM) kills. When
    49	a container uses more than its `memory` limit, the kernel may terminate it. However,
    50	terminations only happen when the kernel detects memory pressure. Thus, a
    51	container that over allocates memory may not be immediately killed. This means
    52	`memory` limits are enforced reactively. A container may use more memory than
    53	its `memory` limit, but if it does, it may get killed.
    54	
    55	{{< note >}}
    56	There is an alpha feature `MemoryQoS` which attempts to add more preemptive
    57	limit enforcement for memory (as opposed to reactive enforcement by the OOM
    58	killer). However, this effort is
    59	[stalled](https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/tree/a47155b340/keps/sig-node/2570-memory-qos#latest-update-stalled)
    60	due to a potential livelock situation a memory hungry can cause.
    61	{{< /note >}}
    62	
    63	{{< note >}}
    64	If you specify a limit for a resource, but do not specify any request, and no admission-time
    65	mechanism has applied a default request for that resource, then Kubernetes copies the limit
    66	you specified and uses it as the requested value for the resource.
    67	{{< /note >}}

    71	*CPU* and *memory* are each a *resource type*. A resource type has a base unit.
    72	CPU represents compute processing and is specified in units of [Kubernetes CPUs](#meaning-of-cpu).
    73	Memory is specified in units of bytes.
    74	For Linux workloads, you can specify _huge page_ resources.
    75	Huge pages are a Linux-specific feature where the node kernel allocates blocks of memory
    76	that are much larger than the default page size.
    77	
    78	For example, on a system where the default page size is 4KiB, you could specify a limit,
    79	`hugepages-2Mi: 80Mi`. If the container tries allocating over 40 2MiB huge pages (a

    83	You cannot overcommit `hugepages-*` resources.
    84	This is different from the `memory` and `cpu` resources.

    89	consumed. They are distinct from

    74	Figure 1. HorizontalPodAutoscaler controls the scale of a Deployment and its ReplicaSet
    75	
    76	Kubernetes implements horizontal pod autoscaling as a control loop that runs intermittently
    77	(it is not a continuous process). The interval is set by the
    78	`--horizontal-pod-autoscaler-sync-period` parameter to the
    79	[`kube-controller-manager`](/docs/reference/command-line-tools-reference/kube-controller-manager/)
    80	(and the default interval is 15 seconds).
    81	
    82	Once during each period, the controller manager queries the resource utilization against the
    83	metrics specified in each HorizontalPodAutoscaler definition. The controller manager
    84	finds the target resource defined by the `scaleTargetRef`,
    85	then selects the pods based on the target resource's `.spec.selector` labels,
    86	and obtains the metrics from either the resource metrics API (for per-pod resource metrics),
    87	or the custom metrics API (for all other metrics).
    88	
    89	- For per-pod resource metrics (like CPU), the controller fetches the metrics
    90	  from the resource metrics API for each Pod targeted by the HorizontalPodAutoscaler.
    91	  Then, if a target utilization value is set, the controller calculates the utilization
    92	  value as a percentage of the equivalent
    93	  [resource request](/docs/concepts/configuration/manage-resources-containers/#requests-and-limits)
    94	  on the containers in each Pod. If a target raw value is set, the raw metric values are used directly.
    95	  The controller then takes the mean of the utilization or the raw value (depending on the type
    96	  of target specified) across all targeted Pods, and produces a ratio used to scale
    97	  the number of desired replicas.
    98	
    99	  Please note that if some of the Pod's containers do not have the relevant resource request set,
   100	  CPU utilization for the Pod will not be defined and the autoscaler will
   101	  not take any action for that metric. See the [algorithm details](#algorithm-details) section below
   102	  for more information about how the autoscaling algorithm works.
   103	
   104	- For per-pod custom metrics, the controller functions similarly to per-pod resource metrics,
   105	  except that it works with raw values, not utilization values.
   106	
   107	- For object metrics and external metrics, a single metric is fetched, which describes
   108	  the object in question. This metric is compared to the target
   109	  value, to produce a ratio as above. In the `autoscaling/v2` API
   110	  version, this value can optionally be divided by the number of Pods before the
   111	  comparison is made.
   112	
   113	The common use for HorizontalPodAutoscaler is to configure it to fetch metrics from

   130

   138	\end{equation*}
   139	```

   141	For example, if the current metric value is `200m`, and the desired value
   142	is `100m`, the number of replicas will be doubled, since
   143	\\( { 200.0 \div 100.0 } = 2.0 \\).

   145	replicas, since \\( { 50.0 \div 100.0 } = 0.5 \\). The control plane skips any scaling
   146	action if the ratio is sufficiently close to 1.0 (within a globally-configurable
   147	tolerance, 0.1 by default).

   150	the `currentMetricValue` is computed by taking the average of the given
   151	metric across all Pods in the HorizontalPodAutoscaler's scale target.

   170	considers a Pod "not yet ready" if it's unready and transitioned to

96	Kubernetes offers features to help you run highly available applications even when you
    97	introduce frequent voluntary disruptions.
    98	
    99	As an application owner, you can create a PodDisruptionBudget (PDB) for each application.
   100	A PDB limits the number of Pods of a replicated application that are down simultaneously from
   101	voluntary disruptions. For example, a quorum-based application would
   102	like to ensure that the number of replicas running is never brought below the
   103	number needed for a quorum. A web front end might want to
   104	ensure that the number of replicas serving load never falls below a certain
   105	percentage of the total.
   106	
   107	Cluster managers and hosting providers should use tools which
   108	respect PodDisruptionBudgets by calling the [Eviction API](/docs/tasks/administer-cluster/safely-drain-node/#eviction-api)
   109	instead of directly deleting pods or deployments.
   110	
   111	For example, the `kubectl drain` subcommand lets you mark a node as going out of
   112	service. When you run `kubectl drain`, the tool tries to evict all of the Pods on
   113	the Node you're taking out of service. The eviction request that `kubectl` submits on
   114	your behalf may be temporarily rejected, so the tool periodically retries all failed
   115	requests until all Pods on the target node are terminated, or until a configurable timeout
   116	is reached.
   117	
   118	A PDB specifies the number of replicas that an application can tolerate having, relative to how
   119	many it is intended to have.  For example, a Deployment which has a `.spec.replicas: 5` is
   120	supposed to have 5 pods at any given time.  If its PDB allows for there to be 4 at a time,
   121	then the Eviction API will allow voluntary disruption of one (but not two) pods at a time.
   122	
   123	The group of pods that comprise the application is specified using a label selector, the same
   124	as the one used by the application's controller (deployment, stateful-set, etc).
   125	
   126	The "intended" number of pods is computed from the `.spec.replicas` of the workload resource
   127	that is managing those pods. The control plane discovers the owning workload resource by
   128	examining the `.metadata.ownerReferences` of the Pod.
   129	
   130	[Involuntary disruptions](#voluntary-and-involuntary-disruptions) cannot be prevented by PDBs; however they
   131	do count against the budget.
   132	
   133	Pods which are deleted or unavailable due to a rolling upgrade to an application do count
   134	against the disruption budget, but workload resources (such as Deployment and StatefulSet)
   135	are not limited by PDBs when doing rolling upgrades. Instead, the handling of failures
   136	during application updates is configured in the spec for the specific workload resource.
   137	
   138	It is recommended to set `AlwaysAllow` [Unhealthy Pod Eviction Policy](/docs/tasks/run-application/configure-pdb/#unhealthy-pod-eviction-policy)
   139	to your PodDisruptionBudgets to support eviction of misbehaving applications during a node drain.
   140	The default behavior is to wait for the application pods to become [healthy](/docs/tasks/run-application/configure-pdb/#healthiness-of-a-pod)
   141	before the drain can proceed.
   142	
   143	When a pod is evicted using the eviction API, it is gracefully
   144	[terminated](/docs/concepts/workloads/pods/pod-lifecycle/#pod-termination), honoring the
   145	`terminationGracePeriodSeconds` setting in its [PodSpec](/docs/reference/generated/kubernetes-api/{{< param "version" >}}/#podspec-v1-core).

   311	## Protect slow starting containers with startup probes {#define-startup-probes}
   312	
   313	Sometimes, you have to deal with applications that require additional startup
   314	time on their first initialization. In such cases, it can be tricky to set up
   315	liveness probe parameters without compromising the fast response to deadlocks
   316	that motivated such a probe. The solution is to set up a startup probe with the
   317	same command, HTTP or TCP check, with a `failureThreshold * periodSeconds` long
   318	enough to cover the worst case startup time.
   319	
   320	So, the previous example would become:
   321	
   322	```yaml
   323	ports:
   324	- name: liveness-port
   325	  containerPort: 8080
   326	
   327	livenessProbe:
   328	  httpGet:
   329	    path: /healthz
   330	    port: liveness-port
   331	  failureThreshold: 1
   332	  periodSeconds: 10
   333	
   334	startupProbe:
   335	  httpGet:
   336	    path: /healthz
   337	    port: liveness-port
   338	  failureThreshold: 30
   339	  periodSeconds: 10
   340	```
   341	
   342	Thanks to the startup probe, the application will have a maximum of 5 minutes
   343	(30 * 10 = 300s) to finish its startup.
   344	Once the startup probe has succeeded once, the liveness probe takes over to
   345	provide a fast response to container deadlocks.
   346	If the startup probe never succeeds, the container is killed after 300s and
   347	subject to the pod's `restartPolicy`.
   348	
   394	[Probes](/docs/reference/generated/kubernetes-api/{{< param "version" >}}/#probe-v1-core)
   395	have a number of fields that you can use to more precisely control the behavior of startup,
   396	liveness and readiness checks:
   397	
   398	* `initialDelaySeconds`: Number of seconds after the container has started before startup,
   399	  liveness or readiness probes are initiated. If a startup  probe is defined, liveness and
   400	  readiness probe delays do not begin until the startup probe has succeeded. If the value of
   401	  `periodSeconds` is greater than `initialDelaySeconds` then the `initialDelaySeconds` will be
   402	  ignored. Defaults to 0 seconds. Minimum value is 0.
   403	* `periodSeconds`: How often (in seconds) to perform the probe. Default to 10 seconds.
   404	  The minimum value is 1.
   405	  While a container is not Ready, the `ReadinessProbe` may be executed at times other than
   406	  the configured `periodSeconds` interval. This is to make the Pod ready faster.
   407	* `timeoutSeconds`: Number of seconds after which the probe times out.
   408	  Defaults to 1 second. Minimum value is 1.
   409	* `successThreshold`: Minimum consecutive successes for the probe to be considered successful
   410	  after having failed. Defaults to 1. Must be 1 for liveness and startup Probes.
   411	  Minimum value is 1.
   412	* `failureThreshold`: After a probe fails `failureThreshold` times in a row, Kubernetes
   413	  considers that the overall check has failed: the container is _not_ ready/healthy/live.
   414	  Defaults to 3. Minimum value is 1.
   415	  For the case of a startup or liveness probe, if at least `failureThreshold` probes have
   416	  failed, Kubernetes treats the container as unhealthy and triggers a restart for that
   417	  specific container. The kubelet honors the setting of `terminationGracePeriodSeconds`
   418	  for that container.
   419	  For a failed readiness probe, the kubelet continues running the container that failed
   420	  checks, and also continues to run more probes; because the check failed, the kubelet
   421	  sets the `Ready` [condition](/docs/concepts/workloads/pods/pod-lifecycle/#pod-conditions)
   422	  on the Pod to `false`.
   423	* `terminationGracePeriodSeconds`: configure a grace period for the kubelet to wait between
   424	  triggering a shut down of the failed container, and then forcing the container runtime to stop
   425	  that container.
   426	  The default is to inherit the Pod-level value for `terminationGracePeriodSeconds`

**Decision memo: revise the design before production rollout.** Kubernetes provides controls for disruption, scheduling, health, security, and storage lifecycle. Their presence does not establish application availability or database safety. The recommendations below distinguish documented behavior from choices requiring validation. All citations refer to the supplied local documentation.

1. **The PDB does not guarantee five available replicas in all three cases.** Involuntary node failures cannot be prevented by PDBs, although unavailable Pods count against the budget. During an ordinary node drain using the Eviction API, `minAvailable: 5` limits permitted evictions; requests can be rejected and retried. Direct deletion bypasses that protection. Deployment rolling updates also bypass PDB enforcement, so `maxUnavailable: 2` permits availability to fall to four. Recommend `maxUnavailable: 1`, `maxSurge: 1`, with capacity for surge Pods. This makes rollout policy compatible with five available replicas at desired scale six, without guaranteeing protection against concurrent failures. Sources: [disruptions.md, lines 99–145](docs/concepts/workloads/pods/disruptions.md#L99-L145); [deployment.md, lines 1185–1211](docs/concepts/workloads/controllers/deployment.md#L1185-L1211).

2. **Configure explicit zone spreading and choose the outage tradeoff.** Use the API’s shared labels as `labelSelector`, `topologyKey: topology.kubernetes.io/zone`, and `maxSkew: 1`, targeting two replicas per zone. `topologyKey` groups nodes by label value. With `DoNotSchedule`, skew limits the target domain’s matching-Pod count relative to the global minimum; violating placements remain unscheduled. `ScheduleAnyway` instead prefers placements reducing skew, allowing imbalance. Recommend the latter if restoring capacity during zone loss takes priority over strict balance. Hard constraints can block replacements when an unavailable domain remains counted. If it disappears from eligibility, calculations change; `minDomains: 3` explicitly makes the global minimum zero when fewer than three domains qualify. Neither mode guarantees continuous balance after Pod removal. Sources: [topology-spread-constraints.md, lines 82–130](docs/concepts/scheduling-eviction/topology-spread-constraints.md#L82-L130), [167–185](docs/concepts/scheduling-eviction/topology-spread-constraints.md#L167-L185), [605–619](docs/concepts/scheduling-eviction/topology-spread-constraints.md#L605-L619).

3. **Separate startup completion, traffic eligibility, and restart detection.** Configure a startup probe whose `failureThreshold × periodSeconds` covers measured worst-case startup. Until it succeeds, other probes are disabled; their initial delays begin afterward. Use readiness to establish whether the API can serve useful requests, including required database availability where appropriate. Readiness failure removes the Pod from matching Service endpoints but leaves its container running. Use liveness for an application failure that restarting can resolve, rather than making database unavailability automatically restart every API replica. Startup or liveness failure at its configured threshold triggers container shutdown/restart according to restart policy. Sources: [configure-liveness-readiness-startup-probes.md, lines 311–347](docs/tasks/configure-pod-container/configure-liveness-readiness-startup-probes.md#L311-L347), [398–422](docs/tasks/configure-pod-container/configure-liveness-readiness-startup-probes.md#L398-L422); [pod-lifecycle.md, lines 479–497](docs/concepts/workloads/pods/pod-lifecycle.md#L479-L497), [524–528](docs/concepts/workloads/pods/pod-lifecycle.md#L524-L528).

4. **Thirty seconds is a shutdown budget, not a request-completion guarantee.** The grace-period countdown begins before `preStop`; the hook consumes that budget. The kubelet runs the hook, then requests TERM delivery to the container’s main process. A still-running hook can receive a one-off two-second extension. Remaining processes receive SIGKILL when grace expires. Endpoint handling proceeds concurrently: terminating EndpointSlice entries are not immediately removed, but have `ready: false`; `serving` can support draining-aware consumers. Implement signal handling and connection draining, then size grace for hook time and outstanding work. The documentation does not establish that this application’s long requests finish within thirty seconds. Sources: [pod-v1.md, lines 1006–1008](docs/reference/kubernetes-api/workload-resources/pod-v1.md#L1006-L1008); [pod-lifecycle.md, lines 581–639](docs/concepts/workloads/pods/pod-lifecycle.md#L581-L639).

5. **Set resource requests and limits deliberately.** CPU requests inform scheduling and establish the denominator for CPU-utilization HPA; they are not CPU ceilings. Containers may exceed requests when resources permit. CPU limits cause throttling. Memory limits are enforced reactively through OOM kills, rather than CPU-style throttling, and exceeding a memory limit need not cause immediate termination. For Pod CPU-utilization scaling, missing relevant requests on some containers makes utilization undefined and prevents action for that metric. Specify requests for every relevant container and verify admitted values: when a limit exists without a request or admission default, Kubernetes copies the limit into the request. Sources: [manage-resources-containers.md, lines 18–66](docs/concepts/configuration/manage-resources-containers.md#L18-L66); [horizontal-pod-autoscale.md, lines 89–102](docs/tasks/run-application/horizontal-pod-autoscale.md#L89-L102).

6. **Expect HPA decisions to differ from the raw CPU ratio.** The basic calculation rounds up current replicas multiplied by current/desired metrics, with default tolerance 0.1. Missing metrics are conservatively assumed at 100% of target for downscaling and 0% for upscaling. Not-yet-ready Pods are set aside; when evaluating an otherwise indicated upscale, they are assumed at 0%, dampening it. Recalculation can cancel scaling if direction reverses or falls within tolerance. CPU readiness classification uses configurable defaults of thirty seconds for initial readiness delay and five minutes for initialization. Downscaling uses the highest recommendation within the default five-minute stabilization window. These mechanisms and startup delay mean CPU HPA is not immediate capacity insurance. Sources: [horizontal-pod-autoscale.md, lines 129–218](docs/tasks/run-application/horizontal-pod-autoscale.md#L129-L218).

7. **Replace default allow with explicit ingress and egress allowances.** Select all relevant Pods with default-deny policies for both directions. Then permit authorized callers to the API port, API egress to database destinations/ports, and database ingress from API Pods. Permit DNS egress to the actual cluster resolver, including its required UDP/TCP ports; the documented kube-dns example exposes both on port 53. Ingress and egress isolation are independent, and both connection ends must allow establishment. Policies are additive unions: an existing broad allow cannot be overridden by adding deny policies. A NetworkPolicy-capable CNI implementation is a prerequisite; creating objects without enforcement has no effect. Sources: [network-policies.md, lines 45–81](docs/concepts/services-networking/network-policies.md#L45-L81), [210–259](docs/concepts/services-networking/network-policies.md#L210-L259); [dns-debugging-resolution.md, lines 158–173](docs/tasks/administer-cluster/dns-debugging-resolution.md#L158-L173).

8. **Base64 is insufficient protection for credentials in Git.** The documentation explicitly describes a base64-encoded credential as “obscured but not secret.” Remove readable credentials from committed manifests and adopt a controlled delivery mechanism. Enable Secret encryption at rest: Secrets are stored unencrypted in etcd by default. Apply least-privilege RBAC and restrict which containers receive credentials. Review workload-creation permissions as carefully as direct Secret reads: permission to create Pods in a namespace, including indirectly through Deployments, permits access to that namespace’s Secrets. Encryption at rest does not establish confidentiality for copies committed to Git. Sources: [secret.md, lines 35–48](docs/concepts/configuration/secret.md#L35-L48), [305–307](docs/concepts/configuration/secret.md#L305-L307), [453–457](docs/concepts/configuration/secret.md#L453-L457).

9. **Existing PVs retain their own reclaim policy.** Changing the StorageClass policy is not a retroactive update; inspect and patch existing PVs separately. Dynamically provisioned PVs inherit the class policy, whose default is `Delete`. After PVC deletion, `Retain` leaves the released PV and data for manual reclamation. With supporting plugins, `Delete` removes both PV and backing storage. StatefulSet deletion or scale-down is a separate trigger: PVC retention defaults to `Retain`. Optional `whenDeleted` and `whenScaled: Delete` settings delete affected template PVCs, after which PV reclaim policy matters; the documented feature gate must be enabled. Sources: [storage-classes.md, lines 126–135](docs/concepts/storage/storage-classes.md#L126-L135); [persistent-volumes.md, lines 178–210](docs/concepts/storage/persistent-volumes.md#L178-L210); [statefulset.md, lines 387–423](docs/concepts/workloads/controllers/statefulset.md#L387-L423).

10. **Prioritize validation before increasing exposure.** First, secure credentials and verify existing PV policies and recovery procedures. Second, establish CNI enforcement, DNS/database allowances, and negative connectivity tests. Third, measure startup and shutdown, configure probes/resources, and verify the metrics API prerequisite. Fourth, keep HPA’s minimum at six if six is the operational baseline, configure spreading and compatible rollout limits, then test rollout, drain, node loss, zone loss, and autoscaling under load.

    Release criteria must include limits these documents do not guarantee: useful throughput with five or four survivors; completion of long requests during termination; database failover and recoverability; and actual spare capacity and policy enforcement. Sources: [horizontal-pod-autoscale.md, lines 29–31](docs/tasks/run-application/horizontal-pod-autoscale.md#L29-L31), [113–118](docs/tasks/run-application/horizontal-pod-autoscale.md#L113-L118); [disruptions.md, lines 130–136](docs/concepts/workloads/pods/disruptions.md#L130-L136); [pod-lifecycle.md, lines 619–639](docs/concepts/workloads/pods/pod-lifecycle.md#L619-L639).
